purpose: Valsartan is used to treat high blood pressure, which helps lower your risk of stroke and heart attack. It is also used to treat heart failure and to protect your kidneys, especially if you have diabetes. Keeping your blood pressure under control helps your heart and blood vessels stay healthier longer.
how_it_works: Your body makes a chemical called angiotensin II that squeezes your blood vessels tight, raising your blood pressure. Valsartan blocks the receptors that this chemical attaches to, so your blood vessels can relax and open up. When your blood vessels are more relaxed, your heart does not have to work as hard and your blood pressure goes down.
common_side_effects: Some people feel dizzy, especially when standing up quickly, so take your time when getting up. You might also notice mild tiredness, a runny or stuffy nose, or an upset stomach. Unlike some similar medicines, valsartan is less likely to cause a dry cough.
warnings: Do not take valsartan if you are pregnant or trying to become pregnant, as it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Avoid taking it with potassium supplements or salt substitutes unless your doctor says it is okay, because it can raise your potassium levels too high. Tell your doctor right away if you feel faint, have swelling of your face or throat, or notice a big drop in how much you urinate.
typical_dosing: For high blood pressure, the usual starting dose is 80 to 160 mg once a day, and your doctor may increase it up to 320 mg per day if needed. For heart failure, dosing typically starts at 40 mg twice a day and is slowly increased. Try to take it at the same time each day, with or without food, and never stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
